C1.idea: Developers on two or three squads at once pay a switching cost; the fewer things in progress, the faster each finishes
'Nobody idle' optimises utilisation, not flow; pull work from a limited queue instead of pushing to keep people busy
Overflowing sprints: plan to a forecast the team owns, not a target set from above; the Sprint Goal and commitment belong to the Developers
Difficult goals raise effort, but only with commitment and ability; a target with a bonus attached invites gaming the measure
Output isn't outcome: more features shipped doesn't mean the problem customers care about gets solved; feature bloat
A shared Definition of Done is the quality bar; work that doesn't meet it isn't released, which is where the marketing-engineering argument gets settled
Naming and punishing the developer who merged the release: a just-culture test asks whether a peer would have done the same, and treats the system that let it through as the finding
Blame drives reporting underground; the next near-miss won't be surfaced
Buying tools to 'do both' is a fix that fails or shifts the burden: it eases the symptom and leaves the overload in place
The first change is one constraint, not a programme: cut work in progress (or stop the stretch target), then look again
A disagreement among the sources: goal theory says difficult goals improve performance; the flow and respect-for-people sources say overload and unsustainable pace destroy it

C2.idea: Commander's intent and mission tactics: state the task and its purpose, prescribe method only as far as coordination needs, against cascading KPIs that prescribe outputs
Subordinates should understand intent two levels up
Friction and uncertainty are the normal condition; plans that assume otherwise deny the nature of the work
No zero-defects mentality: be lenient on bold errors and severe on inaction, against appraisal systems that punish visible mistakes
Deference to expertise and a reluctance to simplify: decisions migrate to whoever knows most, not to rank
Preoccupation with failure: treat weak signals and near-misses as data, against dashboards that report green
Normalization of deviance and schedule pressure: a success record is not evidence of safety; Columbia's foam
An independent technical authority or safety function with its own line, not one that reports to the programme it checks
Work as imagined versus work as done; learn why the action made sense at the time, not who broke the rule
The after-action review: leaders enter the discussion only when necessary, it is permissible to disagree, no critique or lecture
What the textbooks teach that the doctrine contradicts: management by objectives and goal cascades; control systems; change managed through a programme
A disagreement among the doctrine sources: the war-fighting doctrine prizes tempo, boldness and accepting risk; the high-reliability sources prize redundancy, verification and stopping when unsure
Simple, complicated, complex: the playbook fits the complicated case and fails in the complex one
